Q: Move Constructor giving me a Debug Assertion Fail A:

In VectorContainer::operator=, you are using delete instead of delete[], which is Undefined Behavior. You MUST match new[] to delete[], and new to delete.

Also, VectorContainer::operator= is returning a VectorContainer* pointer, but it should be returning a VectorContainer& reference instead.

On a side note, there are a number of other issues with your ode:

  • SpitVector() is returning a reference to a local variable. This is Undefined Behavior as the caller will receive a dangling reference to freed memory. You can simply return the local variable by value instead, and get rid of std::move() in the caller. Let the compiler optimize the return value for you.

  • in VectorContainer's Copy Constructor, a[0] needs to be a[i] instead.

  • VectorContainer::pushBack(double d, int a) is mis-named. In standard containers, pushing a value adds a new element to the end of the container, but that is nt not what you are actually doing.

  • The non-const version of VectorContainer::operator[] should return the double by reference, not by value. That will allow assigning values to array elements.

  • The const version of VectorContainer::operator[] returns a double by value, so specifying const on the value is redundant.

Q: Triggering VS Code extension command by some preexisting command A:

No, there is no native way to accomplish this today, because there is no event in the VS Code API that tells you when some command was executed.

But, if what you need is something more abstract like any command or any inline completion, I would suggest you to open a feature request in the VS Code repo (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues), so the team could evaluate exposing an API that would handle this.

On the other hand, if you need know when some command(s) from some specific extension is executed, I would suggest you get in touch with the extension authors, because they can provide their own API extension as well, and you could simply use it on your extension. More info https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/vscode-api#extensions .

Q: What is the scope of a PostgreSQL temp table? A:

Temp tables in PostgreSQL are local only and related to session where they are created. So no sessions (clients) can see temp tables from other sessions. Both schema and data are invisible to others. Your code is safe.

Q: Azure Blob Storage A:

Single Container vs. Per-User Containers

Your senior's advice is a common pattern, but it's not a universal best practice — it's a trade-off. The two main models are:

Single container, prefixed blobs (e.g. user_123/photo.jpg)

  • Simpler IAM setup — one SAS token policy to rule them all

  • Cheaper (Azure charges per storage transaction, not per container)

  • Scales to millions of users without hitting limits

  • Harder to isolate users for billing, quotas, or deletion

Per-user containers (e.g. container user-123, blob photo.jpg)

  • Clean isolation — easy to delete all of a user's data, set per-user policies, generate scoped SAS tokens

  • Azure allows up to 5,000 containers per storage account, so this only works if your user count is bounded and known

  • Better fit for lease-based workflows (as you already identified)

For a true multi-tenant service with potentially large or unbounded user counts, the single container + prefix model is the standard recommendation from Microsoft's own architecture guidance. For a bounded internal tool or B2B product, per-container is often cleaner.

Blob Leases

You cannot acquire a lease on a list of blobs or a prefix — leases are per-blob or per-container only. There is no "lease this logical folder" concept in the Azure Blob Storage API.

In the single-container model, a container lease would indeed serialize all writes across all users, which is almost certainly not what you want. Your options for concurrency control per-user are:

  • Per-blob leases: Acquire a lease on a specific blob before writing/deleting it. This is the correct granularity for optimistic locking in a shared container. The azure_storage_blobs crate exposes this via BlobLeaseClient.

  • ETags + conditional writes: Use if_match conditions on put/delete operations instead of leases. This is often simpler for high-throughput scenarios and doesn't require explicit lease management or renewal.

  • Application-level locking: Use Redis, a DB row lock, or similar if your locking semantics are more complex than what blob leases support.

Prefix Listing

Yes, you absolutely can list blobs by prefix — and you should. This is the idiomatic way to implement "virtual folders" in a flat blob namespace:

rust

let prefix = format!("user_{}/", user_id);

let mut stream = container_client
    .list_blobs()
    .prefix(Cow::Owned(prefix))  // filters server-side
    .into_stream();

while let Some(page) = stream.next().await {
    let page = page?;
    for blob in page.blobs.items {
        println!("{}", blob.name);
    }
}

A few things worth noting here:

  • The prefix filter is applied server-side, so you're not pulling all blobs and filtering in memory — this is efficient.

  • The .into_stream() already handles pagination for you. Each .next() call fetches one page (up to 5,000 blobs by default). The comment about "eventually paginate" in your boilerplate is unnecessary if you're using the stream correctly — it's already lazy and paginated. The only concern would be if someone is calling .collect() on the stream and loading everything into memory at once.

  • You can also pass a delimiter (typically /) alongside the prefix to get a "directory listing" view, which returns BlobPrefix entries instead of recursing into sub-prefixes. Useful if you have nested virtual directories.

Summary Recommendation

For your use case, I'd suggest:

  1. Keep the single container — it's the right call for scalability.

  2. Prefix all blobs with the user ID — {user_id}/{blob_name} — and use prefix-scoped listing.

  3. Drop the container lease — it's not useful here. Use per-blob leases or ETag-based conditional requests for write safety.

  4. Fix the pagination — make sure you're iterating the stream lazily rather than collecting it entirely, and you won't hit result limits regardless of blob count.

Q: How can I resolve this dangling pointer situation? A:

There are multiple issues in the posted code:

  • the destination address defined as uint8_t address only has 8 bits. This is seems unlikely so you might want to check this prototype.
  • given that mydata16b is volatile, it will be read twice to initialize the array myArray as uint8_t myArray[3] = {mydata8b, mydata16b, mydata16b >> 8}; You might want to use an intermediary local variable to only read the global variable once, hence ensure that the values of the high and lo bytes are consistent.
  • if the SerWrite handler just copies the pointer to static memory and handles the data asynchronously, you basically have no safe way to determine when to free the array or reuse it. You could allocate memory for this and worry about freeing later or use a static array if you can ensure MyWriteFun is not called again until the data has been sent. Such an API is very error prone.
